title: Wasps: Not as cute as bees
summary: Josh and Chuck explore wasps as an insect group: body plan (head, thorax, abdomen, narrow waist), evolution from Cretaceous predators into pollinators, the diet shift from carnivory to nectar and pollen, and why adult wasps feed larvae insects they paralyze. They cover the stinger's origin as a modified ovipositor, the chemical makeup of wasp venom and why stings hurt so much, nest types (paper wasp, bald-faced hornet, mud dauber, yellow jacket, solitary vs. social colonies and queens), the tarantula hawk, and the Asian giant hornet ("murder hornet") threat to European honeybees. They argue wasps are beneficial pollinators and pest controllers, cite low US/UK/Australia sting death figures, give advice on avoiding and removing nests, and describe Japanese wasp larva hunting. The episode ends with a listener mail about a They Might Be Giants reference.
topics: wasps as pollinators and pest control

segments.title: Book promo and opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts plug their upcoming book, then introduce the wasp episode, inspired by a Robert Lamb article, and mention Lamb's other podcasts. They share a story about a fallen wasp nest in Chuck's yard.

segments.title: Why wasps get a bad rap and body anatomy
segments.summary: The hosts discuss why wasps are disliked compared with bees, including painful stings and their predatory role. They note there are over 20,000 species, that hornets are a type of wasp, and describe the three body segments, antennae, eyes, the narrow waist, and the stinger in females.

segments.title: Wasp evolution, the Cretaceous, and the shift to pollination
segments.summary: The hosts trace wasp origins to Cretaceous predators that ate spiders and insects, and how the rise of flowering plants (angiosperms) led wasps to shift toward pollen and nectar. Adult wasps became partly herbivorous while still feeding larvae insect prey.

segments.title: Stinger origins and wasp venom
segments.summary: The stinger evolved from the ovipositor used to lay eggs in prey. The venom is a cocktail of compounds (enzymes, histamines, neurotoxic and pain-triggering peptides, an antimicrobial agent) that causes intense, prolonged pain and paralyzes prey. Wasps can sting repeatedly, and an expert estimate is about ten stings on average for a person.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break before the nesting segment.

segments.title: Asian giant hornet threat and personal sting stories
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Asian giant hornets (murder hornets) in the Pacific Northwest, a 2016 intercepted shipment at San Francisco airport, and their threat to European honey bees, which lack the heat-balling defense of Asian honey bees. They compare the hornet's venom potency and pain, and Josh recounts being stung eleven times while hiking near an underground nest.

segments.title: Nest types and social vs solitary wasps
segments.summary: The hosts describe common nest types: paper wasp and bald-faced hornet paper nests, the large gray hornet nests kept as decor, and mud dauber mud tubes. They explain solitary wasps versus social colonies with queens, drones, and workers, and how queens overwinter and rebuild colonies. Yellow jacket nests can have multiple queens with hierarchy, and wasps release alarm pheromones.

segments.title: Tarantula hawk and wasp prey paralysis
segments.summary: The tarantula hawk lays eggs in a paralyzed tarantula, and larvae eat it from the inside. Most wasps paralyze insects and leave them alive for their larvae. Charles Darwin is cited as finding this troubling. Farmers may value wasps for pest control.

segments.title: Wasps as pollinators, sting death statistics, and avoidance tips
segments.summary: The hosts argue wasps are useful pollinators and pest controllers and should not be killed indiscriminately. They cite US, UK, and Australian sting death figures, compare them to ladder falls, and offer advice on avoiding attracting wasps and on hiring professionals to remove nests.

segments.title: Japanese wasp larva hunting
segments.summary: Japanese enthusiasts catch wasps by baiting them with raw fish tied to a string, track them to nests, raise the larvae, and eat them in the fall.

segments.title: Listener mail: They Might Be Giants reference
segments.summary: A listener writes that the hosts missed a They Might Be Giants reference about Stanboul versus Constantinople in an earlier episode. Josh promises a joke for him.
